findings.issue: contradicts task clause "The comments state what the code now does": gate_red_lines' docstring still says "a background gate's red reaches its reader as a repeat every time, so a reader taking the first GATE line would name the banner as the red". After this diff a background red is read back by recorded_red from its row and carries no GATE VERDICT REUSED banner at all, so the stated reason for the banner filter is no longer true of the path it names (the filter still serves a green-then-red second ask).
findings.resolution: Reword the docstring to say the banner can open a repeated verdict (a second ask that repeated a red) and that a background red is no longer one of those.

findings.issue: contradicts task clause "The comments state what the code now does": the module docstring still says of a background gate that "the verdict is that row's, repeated rather than measured again". After the diff a red is the row's own verdict with nothing asked, and a green is asked again and may measure the entries that name the plan, so "repeated rather than measured again" is the wording this task set out to correct.
findings.resolution: Say: a red is acted on as its row records it; a green is asked again, repeating each step that grades the tree and measuring an entry naming a path the identity leaves out.

findings.issue: The read-back clause embeds each measured step's name, which is the gate entry's command text, unbounded and unsanitised. The outcome claims the did clauses hold no ` | ` and no `; `; that holds for the fixtures only. The signal line flattens ` | ` (_flat in did_word_clause), but a command containing `; ` is joined into a `; `-separated field, and a long command makes fit_rest drop the whole clause to `+N` in the signal line, so the detail acceptance (1)/(2) asks for survives only in the printed text.
findings.resolution: Clip each step name in step_seconds/repeated to a fixed width and replace `; ` in names, or state in the outcome that the clause is carried whole only in the printed text.
